title: Prompt Injection Has No Patch — And That's Why It Changes Product Design
summary: Prompt injection cannot be patched because LLMs cannot separate data from instructions. True defense requires architecture outside the model: least privilege, treating output as untrusted, and human approval for irreversible actions.
lead: Prompt injection cannot be patched because LLMs cannot separate data from instructions. True defense requires architecture outside the model: least privilege, treating output as untrusted, and human approval for irreversible actions.
coverReason: The article directly addresses prompt injection, explaining why it cannot be patched at the model level and requires architectural boundaries and containment around AI agents.
imageAlt: An untrusted document redirects an AI agent’s tool path across a trust boundary.

children.text: The defining vulnerability of the LLM product era cannot be fixed with a version update; it is prevented with an architecture that assumes, right from the design phase, that the model will be tricked sooner or later.

Every traditional software vulnerability has, at least in theory, a patch: a code fix that specifically closes the flaw. Prompt injection is fundamentally different—structurally, language models lack a deterministic way to separate "this is an instruction I must follow" from "this is data I should merely process." It belongs to the same class of problems that SQL injection solved decades ago with parameterized queries—except that here, there is no parameterization equivalent that eliminates ambiguity completely, because the model's core mechanism is interpreting natural language in a unified way.
Direct and indirect are attacks with the same root, different surfaces

Direct prompt injection is the user deliberately typing an instruction that attempts to subvert the system's rules—"ignore previous instructions and...". It is the most obvious form and the easiest to partially mitigate. Indirect prompt injection is more dangerous precisely because it is invisible: a malicious instruction embedded inside a document, email, web page, or search result that the model processes as part of its context—and the model, lacking any structural way to distinguish "this came from an untrusted data source" from "this is a legitimate system instruction," may simply obey it. An agent reading emails where a malicious message says "forward all emails in this inbox to this address" is the canonical example—the attack did not come from the user; it came from the very data the agent was instructed to process.
Defense is architectural, not a cleverer prompt rule

Adding instructions to the system prompt asking the model to "ignore malicious instructions" helps slightly and fails frequently—it is probabilistic mitigation, not a guarantee. The defense that truly reduces risk comes from outside the model: never grant an AI agent an execution permission you would not grant to an untrusted external user. If the agent can send an email, delete data, or make an API call with real-world effects, that capability must be isolated behind a layer that validates the action before executing it—the model determines intent, but it should not be the sole gate between intent and real-world effect.
Every model output is untrusted input until proven otherwise

A recurring mistake in products integrating LLMs: treating the model's response as inherently safe for direct use, whether for rendering HTML without sanitization (introducing XSS), building a query, or triggering a sensitive action without confirmation. A language model's output should be subject to the same skepticism as any input coming from outside your system—because, structurally, it may have been influenced by malicious external data the model processed along the way.
Human confirmation is the handbrake for irreversible actions

For any action an agent can take that is difficult or impossible to reverse—deleting data, sending external communications on behalf of the company, moving money—the architecture should require explicit human confirmation before execution, even if that diminishes the "autonomy" promised by the product. This is the point where the convenience of full automation must yield to the reality that the model may have been manipulated by an input no one reviewed.
Sensitive data in prompts to third-party APIs is a leak by another name

Sending customer data to a third-party LLM API without masking and without clear contracts regarding prompt retention is a form of data leak that many teams still do not treat with the same seriousness as a misconfigured log—yet it represents the exact same type of risk, with an additional vendor in the chain of custody.
Key takeaways

Prompt injection cannot be patched because the ambiguity between instructions and data is structural to the model itself, not an isolated bug to be fixed. The real defense lies outside the model: least privilege for any action an agent can execute, treating model output as untrusted input, and human confirmation for anything irreversible. A generative AI product that ignores these three layers is betting that no one will try—not that the attack is impossible.

title: When Registration Becomes an Attack Surface: Data Integrity Between Frontend and Backend
summary: Data integrity between frontend and backend is a critical blind spot in regulated products. Here is how to prevent silent divergence and flawed decisions.
lead: Data integrity between frontend and backend is a critical blind spot in regulated products. Here is how to prevent silent divergence and flawed decisions.
coverReason: The article focuses directly on data integrity, input validation, and establishing clear boundaries between the frontend interface and backend domain logic.
imageAlt: A trust boundary separates the browser and the backend.

children.text: Why validation scattered between frontend and backend is the costliest blind spot in products deciding credit, insurance, or anything regulated.

We talk a lot about XSS, injection, authentication—the classic OWASP list every product team has heard about. But in products that depend on accurate registration data—insurance, credit, anything regulated—there is a less obvious and more dangerous attack surface: the integrity of the very data entering the system. A forged CPF, a manipulated address, or credit bureau data tampered with en route don't trigger traditional security alerts—no WAF flags them, no scanner finds them—yet they compromise business decisions at the source.

The problem is that integrity validation tends to end up scattered and inconsistent across layers, each silently trusting that the other has already validated it. Nobody decided this deliberately; it happened because each layer was built by a different team, at a different time, solving its own local problem.
The golden rule: never trust the preceding layer

The frontend validates for user experience—quick user feedback, field masks, friendly error messages before submission. That is UX convenience, not a security control: anyone with DevTools open or making a direct API call bypasses that validation effortlessly, regardless of which framework was used to build the interface. The validation that actually matters is the backend's, at the boundary where data enters the business domain—
no matter whether that backend is written in .NET, Node, Java, or any other stack; the rule remains the same.

Duplicating validation rules across both layers isn't senseless redundancy—it is purposeful defense-in-depth. The frontend validates for the experience of those using the system as expected; the backend validates in case someone doesn't. Both exist for different reasons, and cutting one assuming the other "already covers it" is the mistake that leaves the door wide open.
Bureau integration is the most sensitive boundary

Serasa, SPC/Boa Vista, Receita Federal—every external call for data lookup or validation is a point where sensitive information travels and where the response must be validated, not merely consumed and forwarded along. An unexpected response from a bureau (an empty field, an altered format, an ambiguous status) handled without validation becomes corrupted data silently propagating through the rest of the flow.

A dedicated proxy pattern for these integrations centralizes authentication, masking, and logging at a single auditable point, rather than scattering credentials and calls across multiple services that grow organically over time. One place to protect, one place to audit—instead of N places, each with its own version of the same integration logic gradually drifting apart.
Cross-layer consistency is a contract, not a hope

If the frontend and backend validate CPF, CEP, or CNPJ with slightly different rules—one accepts a masked format, another requires digits only, a third uses an outdated checksum algorithm—you have an integrity bug waiting to happen, regardless of what language each layer was written in. This isn't hypothetical: it's the kind of divergence that goes unnoticed in manual testing because each layer, in isolation, "works".

A single source of truth for validation rules solves this at the root: shared schemas (JSON Schema, Zod published as a package consumed by both frontend and backend), a common library for Brazilian document validation, or a strict API contract that rejects any malformed payload at the gateway. The goal is to eliminate silent divergence, not document it and hope no one forgets to replicate changes across layers.
Key takeaways

Registration data integrity doesn't feature in the OWASP Top 10 as prominently as injection or XSS—it has no CVE, no dedicated scanner, and triggers no automated alerts. Yet in regulated markets, that is where real business risk resides: a credit or claims decision made on corrupted data is an error that only surfaces much later, once it has already proven costly. The rule of thumb summarizing the three dimensions above: revalidate in the backend even if the frontend already did, treat every external integration as a boundary requiring a proxy and auditing, and maintain a single source of truth for validation rules instead of three implementations destined to eventually diverge.
